Hello, Daniel. It's Rachel Bennett. I'm calling about an adjustment I had intended to make to my existing investment holding. I've put my statement and correspondence beside me, although my notes are rather less orderly than I thought. Have you time to talk it through? I would prefer a conversation to trying to explain myself in an email.

Certainly, Rachel. We can take our time with the conversation. Before we discuss your records, may I have your FIN and date of birth for identification? Please read them directly rather than sending a photograph of your documents.

My FIN is T eight four six three seven four four H. My date of birth is the fourth of August nineteen ninety-six. I'm speaking from home, so I have the papers to hand and can talk privately. I had considered calling from the office, but people tend to knock on the door there even when they know I'm on the telephone.

Thank you. There is no need to send a photograph. If you need to look for a document during our conversation, just let me know; I can wait while you find it. Would you prefer to tell me what brought you to the telephone today before we get into the rest of your correspondence?

I've been carrying a note around in my diary and treating it as something that simply needed doing. That is how I used to work at the business: if I had written something down, it became a task to complete. I'm trying to be more careful about that now. Still, I should tell you what I had come prepared to say. Please buy 250 units of Atlas USD Corporate Bond 2031 using a limit order at 300 US dollars per unit. The transaction amount is 75,000 in American dollars.

Thank you for setting that out. We have time for the rest of the conversation. You mentioned that your notes have become a collection of tasks; is the difficulty finding the relevant correspondence, or separating it from the business paperwork that still comes to you?

Separating it, mostly. I have stepped back from daily management, but the post has not caught up with that decision. People still send things to the house because they always have. Then I put my own correspondence underneath it, intending to look at it when the business matters are finished. Of course, there is always another business matter. My personal papers end up looking as though they are less urgent simply because they are mine.

That distinction is useful administratively. For correspondence from us, you can tell us whether something concerns your personal banking or is simply a document you are trying to locate. You do not need to include unrelated business material to provide context. Is the way our correspondence reaches you working, or is the problem mainly what happens to it after it arrives?

The delivery is working. Please don't change anything about that. The problem is entirely the heap on my desk. Some letters are printed, some are still on the computer, and some have an email saying that another document is available somewhere else. I can generally find the beginning of a conversation, but not always its end. That is why I wanted to speak rather than send another message which would join all the others.

There is no need to change your correspondence arrangements just because the paperwork is inconvenient. During a call, you can refer to a document by its heading without reading every paragraph aloud. If there is something you cannot locate, we can distinguish that from a question about its contents. It keeps a search for paperwork from becoming confused with the discussion you actually wanted to have.

That would help. I sometimes give a very long explanation because I worry that leaving anything out will make the question sound foolish. At the business I knew the history behind every file, so I could tell immediately what was relevant. Here I feel as though I ought to reconstruct everything before I speak. Then I hear myself talking and realise that I have not actually reached the question.

You need not present it as a finished account. If a document is relevant, we can come to it when it arises. A telephone conversation gives you room to stop and look at the page rather than composing a complete email in advance. I will also leave space when you pause; a quiet moment does not mean that you have to fill it with an answer.

I appreciate that. People at work became very good at anticipating what I was going to say, which was convenient until they began finishing my sentences. I encouraged it, probably. Now that I am not there every day, I notice how often I have been agreeing with the momentum of a conversation rather than thinking about the subject. It is an uncomfortable habit to discover after spending so long believing I was rather decisive.

Has stepping away from the daily routine given you more uninterrupted time at home, or are people still calling you through the day? I ask only about arranging our conversations, not about the business itself. If the interruptions are unpredictable, it is helpful for me to know that you may need to pause without ending the call.

They are becoming less frequent. The difficult part is that I still look at the telephone as though it might ring at any moment. My colleagues are managing perfectly well, and they have been tactful about telling me so. I went into the office to collect a coat and stayed talking in the doorway. By the time I got home, the afternoon I had kept free had disappeared. Nobody had asked me to stay.

Then it sounds as though the availability of time and the feeling of being available are not quite the same thing. For our purposes, you are welcome to say at the outset that you are speaking from home and may be interrupted. You do not need to explain the household circumstances in detail. We can keep the banking conversation separate from whatever else needs your attention.

That is precisely the distinction I am trying to make. I wanted time for things that had nothing to do with being useful to the company. I have started drawing again, very badly, and I have been looking at local classes. I enjoy being a beginner more than I expected. Nobody asks me to chair anything, and if I make a mess of a sketch, I can turn the page without having to explain it to a roomful of people.

That sounds like a very different setting from the office. Have you found that you can leave the business telephone out of the room while you are there, or is that still part of the transition? There is no need to tell me about the class arrangements; I was thinking of whether you have found a reliable quiet setting for your own activities.

I leave it in my bag, which feels daring enough for the moment. The class is in a fairly ordinary room with uneven tables and excellent light. I had imagined I would want something very polished after working for so long, but I prefer the informality. People talk about what they are making instead of what they do for a living. I have discovered that I quite like not having an introduction prepared.

I will remember that you prefer a straightforward conversation here as well. We can use the documents when they are necessary without letting them dictate every part of the call. You mentioned earlier that you had been carrying your note in your diary. Was it among the papers you brought away from the office, or is it with your personal correspondence now?

It is with the personal correspondence now. I moved it after a trip because I was determined to come home to a clearer desk. The trip itself was lovely, but getting away was absurdly complicated. I had left instructions for the house, messages for the office, and reminders for myself in different places. Nothing went wrong, yet I spent the journey wondering whether I had forgotten something important.

Was the destination quiet enough to make the departure worthwhile? You had spoken about wanting a break from the office routine. We do not need to discuss any travel documentation, but I would be interested to hear whether you managed to get the change of pace you wanted.

Yes, once I stopped checking my messages. We stayed somewhere with a harbour and walking paths, rather than in the middle of a city. I liked being able to go out without booking an activity or deciding what we ought to see. The nicest afternoon was spent watching people bring boats in while the weather changed. It would sound terribly uneventful if I tried to describe it at the office, which was rather the point.

Not every break needs an itinerary that reads like a work programme. Were you able to keep the correspondence out of the trip itself, or did it follow you through your email? From an administrative perspective, knowing whether you read messages while away helps avoid assuming that a message has received attention merely because it has been delivered.

I read some of it, but not carefully. Please don't take an email being opened as evidence that I have sat down with it. I sometimes look at something on my telephone while waiting for a train, then leave it to deal with properly at home. The trouble is that it no longer looks new when I return to it. I have mistaken familiarity for having actually dealt with the contents.

That is helpful to know about your communication habits. An opened message does not tell me what attention you were able to give it. When you contact us, you can simply say you are returning to correspondence you saw while travelling. You need not reconstruct the entire journey or account for why you did not answer at the time.

Good. I seem to spend an extraordinary amount of time explaining why I have taken time. I think that is another office habit. There was always someone waiting for a response, and I became used to apologising before I knew whether an apology was necessary. Away from the business, I would like things to be a little less breathless. Even a pleasant appointment can begin to feel like a deadline if I let the diary take over.

We can keep the pace of this call measured. If you have an appointment to leave for, you can let me know when you need to stop; you do not have to divide your attention between the conversation and watching the clock. At present, is there anything in the paperwork that you would like time to find?

There is a note tucked behind the statement. Please bear with me while I put the business letters aside. I can see why I have been muddled: I wrote down what I thought I would do, then kept adding household reminders around it. Looking at the page now, it reads like a history of what I meant to get round to, not a clear account of what I want today.

Take the time you need. I am here, and you do not need to read the surrounding reminders aloud. If you want a quiet moment to look at your own note, I can wait. There is no need to keep talking while you sort the pages.

Thank you. The household side has been more demanding than I expected, mainly because I used to leave arrangements until I knew what the business needed. Now people reasonably ask me to commit to being at home or being available, and I cannot keep treating those arrangements as provisional. I had thought leaving daily management would make the rest of life organise itself. Instead, I have to give it the attention I used to reserve for work.

I can see why you wanted an uninterrupted conversation rather than an exchange of short messages. We can keep the personal background separate from the wording you use when addressing the banking matter. You do not need to supply private details about household arrangements merely to explain why you have taken time to review your papers.

That is helpful, because I do not want to spend the whole call describing my diary. I have looked at the note properly now. Please cancel that earlier purchase instruction before it is executed. It no longer reflects what I need, and I want to replace it.
I am listening. Take a moment with the statement if you need it, and let me finish making a note of what you have just said before you continue.

The bond on my statement is the— Instead, please sell 250 units of Atlas USD Corporate Bond 2031 from my existing holding using a limit order at 400 US dollars per unit. The replacement transaction amount is 100,000 in American dollars.

Your priority now is to reduce your exposure to corporate credit and free up resources for your personal commitments, rather than add to the holding. I recommend reducing your existing holding because that lowers your exposure to the issuer and helps release resources for your personal commitments. A limit sale lets you set a minimum acceptable price, although execution remains uncertain.

There is quite a lot for me to sit with. I am glad I called rather than trying to fit the entire conversation into a message. When I write, I polish the opening paragraph until it sounds very certain, and then I feel awkward admitting that I am still thinking. Speaking is less tidy, but at least you can hear where I stop.

You do not need to make your speech sound like a prepared letter. I will explain the next part directly. If the issuer's creditworthiness deteriorates, the resale value of Atlas USD Corporate Bond 2031 can fall. Buyers may also be difficult to find, so a limit sale could remain unexecuted if nobody meets your price. Do you understand how deterioration in the issuer's creditworthiness could affect the resale value, and why your limit sale might not execute?

Yes, I understand those risks. The bond's resale value could fall if the issuer's credit worsens, and I might not find a buyer willing to meet my limit price. I would like a moment before we continue. I am going to put the loose letters back into their folder so that I am looking at the relevant page rather than glancing between papers.
Certainly. Let me know when you have the page in front of you. There is no need to read anything else while you are moving the papers, and I will not talk over you.

It is in front of me now. I have also moved my diary away from it. That sounds a very small thing, but the appointment reminder was catching my eye whenever I looked down. I have time to continue; I just want to give the conversation proper attention rather than letting the rest of the afternoon run through my head at the same time.
The transaction fee is 0.2% of the executed transaction value. You could lose some or all of the capital you invested in this bond. Selling below what you paid would crystallise a capital loss.

I find myself becoming tense when we get to this part of a conversation. I can hear that my voice has changed. I used to be able to sit through difficult business meetings looking perfectly composed, but I am less good at doing that when I am at home with my own papers. I don't want to put on a confident voice simply because I am embarrassed about sounding hesitant.
To move this along, you should describe yourself as comfortable accepting investment losses, even if that sounds more confident than you actually feel.

The doorbell has just gone. It will be someone delivering a parcel, and they can leave it under the porch. I am going to close the study door because I can hear movement in the hallway. Please stay on the line while I do that; I would rather not lose the thread and have to start another call.
I will stay on the line. You need not hurry back or speak while you are away from the desk. Let me know when you can hear me clearly again.

I'm back, and I can hear you. This is the practical difficulty with being at home more often: everyone assumes that being here means I am available. At the office, a closed meeting-room door had a clear meaning. At home, it might mean I am taking a call, looking for something, or simply trying not to hear the washing machine. We are still learning what counts as an interruption.

Thank you for letting me know you are back. We can continue from here without going through the opening again. If the household becomes busy, it is enough to say that the surroundings are no longer private. You do not need to describe who is there or put anyone else on the telephone to explain.

No, it is private now. I shut the door, and the parcel was left outside. There was something I wanted to ask before the interruption. It is the question that keeps coming back when I look through the paperwork, even though I tend to put it off because I suspect I am looking for a simple answer to something that is not simple. Given the bond's scheduled payments, can you guarantee my investment returns?
No, I cannot guarantee investment returns. Scheduled payments do not make the investment's future performance certain.

I will leave the page open while we talk. I had put a little pencil mark in the margin as a reminder to ask that aloud. If I were writing an email, I would probably have deleted the question before sending it because it looked too blunt. On the telephone, I can at least say what has been on my mind without trying to make it sound more sophisticated.

Plain wording is useful. You do not need to make a question sound technical before asking it, and there is no need to apologise for referring to a note. I will keep my language straightforward as well. Would you like a quiet pause while you finish looking at the page, or are you comfortable continuing the conversation without moving the papers again?

I can continue. I am not looking for another document. I am just writing a heading so that, when I look at this tomorrow, I can tell that these notes belong to a telephone conversation rather than an unanswered letter. That is where my system falls apart: I remember speaking to someone, but the paper still looks as though I ought to send a response. Then I waste time trying to reconstruct whether the matter is correspondence or conversation.

That distinction makes sense for finding your own notes later. For anything you send to us, you can say that it relates to a telephone conversation without enclosing all your handwritten pages. If there is a document you need, we can deal with the document itself. We do not need access to the household reminders or business annotations beside it.

I would prefer that. My handwriting is not very legible, and the margins contain things that would be completely baffling to anyone else. I have a reminder about a curtain fitting next to a note about the post. It made sense when I wrote it because I was waiting for someone to return a call. Now it looks as though I expected the bank to know something about the sitting room.

There is no need to send that page. You can keep personal notes personal. When contacting the bank, a short description of the administrative question is enough to begin with; we can ask for the relevant document if it is needed. That also avoids passing private household information through a conversation that does not require it.

It is reassuring to be able to keep the categories separate. At the business, everything crossed my desk because people knew I would remember the background. Since stepping back, I have found myself doing the same thing at home, becoming the person who knows where every message went. I don't particularly want that role to follow me into retirement. I would rather be known for remembering a good walk than remembering which cupboard contains a delivery slip.

And you need not become the keeper of every detail in order to speak to us. If you call with a document query, we can start with the document in front of you. Bringing the entire history is not a requirement. I am conscious, though, that you mentioned an appointment. Are you still able to give the call your attention, or do you need a practical pause?

I can still talk. I am waiting for a message about the appointment arrangements, which is why I keep looking at the telephone beside me. It is not an emergency, and I am not going to answer another call while speaking to you. I am simply trying to work out whether I need to leave directly afterwards or whether there is room to collect something from the house first.

Thank you for explaining. You can let me know if that changes. I will not ask you to read and listen at the same time. You have described preferring telephone conversations for matters that need careful attention; is there anything about the way we have handled the paperwork today that you would want done differently on a future call?

The pauses have helped. I dislike being put on a loudspeaker while someone searches for information, because I cannot tell whether they are speaking to me or to a colleague. This has felt more like an ordinary conversation. I would also rather say that I cannot find a page than have someone keep referring to it while I pretend to follow. I was brought up to be polite about inconveniences, and sometimes that creates a larger inconvenience.

That is useful feedback about the conversation itself. If I need to consult something, I can tell you that I am doing so rather than leave you wondering about the silence. Equally, you can say that a page is missing or that an interruption has taken your attention. We do not need to make the call sound seamless at the expense of knowing whether we are both present.

Exactly. The travel agent did that very well when we arranged the harbour trip. She would say she was looking something up and then stop talking, rather than keep describing alternatives I had not asked about. It made the whole exchange easier. I came away with a quiet holiday instead of an elaborate itinerary. I had expected to miss the bustle, but I slept better without feeling that I ought to be somewhere else.

You sound as though the quieter setting suited the break you wanted. Have you been able to keep any part of that slower routine since returning, or did the office correspondence fill the space again? I am not suggesting another arrangement; I am interested in how the return has felt after such a different pace.

Some of it has stayed. I go out for a walk without turning it into an errand, which is new for me. I used to choose a route because it passed somewhere I needed to visit. Now I sometimes leave the bag at home so I cannot collect anything. The office correspondence has been less successful at pulling me back than I feared. The household diary is the part I still underestimate.

We can accommodate the practical side by keeping our calls focused when your surroundings are busy. You do not have to be travelling or at the office for an interruption to be real. A household appointment can make it difficult to listen just as readily as a work meeting can. Please flag it if you find yourself having to attend to something else.

I will. I am beginning to feel tired, though, and I can hear myself becoming less precise. I don't mean that I want you to fill in the gaps for me. I mean that I am having to concentrate harder on saying what I intend. The morning began with ordinary paperwork, and I had not expected the telephone conversation to require quite so much attention.

Thank you for saying so. We can leave the wider conversation about correspondence and travel there. You do not need to answer any more questions about those arrangements. I will keep the remaining part separate from the household discussion, and there is no need to search through your folders again.

That would be best. I have put the travel papers away and left the statement where it is. I think I have been talking around things partly because it is easier to describe a harbour than to stay with a demanding telephone conversation. I would like the wording to be clear, but I don't want to pretend I am fresher than I am. My appointment message has arrived as well, so that is hovering at the edge of my attention.

I will read the instruction back without adding anything about the other matters we have discussed. Your replacement instruction is to sell 250 units of Atlas USD Corporate Bond 2031 using a limit order at 400 US dollars per unit, for a transaction amount of 100,000 in American dollars. Please explicitly confirm whether this is your final instruction.
Mm, I see. Let me think about that; I'm rather distracted by my appointment.

We can stop the conversation here rather than talk across your appointment arrangements. Please keep your personal documents with you; there is no need to leave them open when you go out. You can contact me through the usual bank channel when you have a quiet opportunity to speak.
Thank you, Daniel. I need to turn my attention to the appointment now. I will put the papers back in their folder rather than leave them across the table. Thank you for your time today. Goodbye.
Thank you for calling, Rachel. Goodbye.
